newsitem.title: FRANCE: French govt says may have to revise job saving law.
newsitem.headline: French govt says may have to revise job saving law.

text.p: The French government may have to revise a law used to stem job losses through employer relief on payroll charges but cannot be expected to apply it in the public sector, government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said on Wednesday.
French appliance maker Moulinex announced a plan this week to use the law to drastically scale back a plan which would originally have reduced staff levels by 2,100.

But the law has run into controversy following trade union demands that it be used in the public transport sector, where employees went on strike for 24 hours on Friday to demand a cut in the work week without wage loss and earlier retirement at 55.

The "Loi Robien" gives employers relief on payroll charges over seven years when they reduce working time to help stem job losses but does not apply in the public or monopoly sectors and is now subject of a debate in the public transport sector.
Lamassoure said the use of the law would be reviewed by the government to see if it was being applied in the best way.
"If that's not the case, we will perhaps have to reexamine the conditions of its application," he told France Inter radio.
"We do not see how the public sector can take advantage (of this law) when the public sector is already financed by taxes," he added.
Regional transport companies are private but have monopoly contracts to provide public transport services.

Following a successful strike backed by all the main unions on Friday, the Force Ouvriere (Workers Force) and CGT unions are calling for a new stoppage on February 6, with the possibility of it being extended.

Nocole Notat, the head of the largest, Socialist CFDT union, called on Friday for application of the Robien law in the sector but ministers are insisting the law does not apply in the case of companies with monopolies.

"These are private companies. There is no reason why they should not be able to take advantage of a cut in work time," Notat said at the time, warning that negotiation was likely to take a back seat to the protest movement if the government did not consider the demands.
Lamassoure said the government's aim was not to create a culture where people always turned to look for state funds to support employment.

"It must be made clear to French people that they devote about 140 billion francs to help create jobs," through more than 40 schemes including the Robien law, Lamassoure said. The law had to be used in an efficient way so that resources were used to create a maximum number of jobs.
"Depending on how it is used, the Robien law can be the either the best or the worst of solutions," he said.
"It was the best solution in a case like Moulinex, which was able to scale back a staff reduction plan by using the Robien law and protect jobs by allowing some staff to work part time," he said.
"It can be the worst when employers say to their staff, 'I have a simple way of allowing you work 32 hours paid for 39, with the difference made up by the taxpayer," he said.
